overview: Buffalo were central to the food, culture, and spiritual life of many Native American tribes before they were nearly wiped out in the 1800s. This bill would direct the Interior Department to help tribes and qualified tribal organizations build and manage buffalo herds on tribal land, through contracts, cooperative agreements, grants, and technical help. The money could support restoration and management programs, buffalo-related businesses, and mobile meat processing facilities. The department would also have to consult tribes on its buffalo policies, including efforts to control diseased animals, keep information tribes mark as culturally sensitive or confidential private, and could give surplus buffalo from federal lands to tribes, waiving the usual charges. The bill leaves federal and state rules on diseased or escaped buffalo in place, does not change treaty rights, and would expire after seven years. As of October 29, 2026, a House committee had approved it and it was placed on the House calendar for a vote.
for: Supporters say the bill gives tribes steady federal support and a formal voice in restoring an animal with deep cultural importance, while also creating food and economic opportunities on tribal land.
against: Critics say growing buffalo herds can raise concerns for nearby ranchers about disease and animals escaping onto neighboring land, and that the bill creates a new grant program without setting a funding level.
